introduction: Bahá’u’lláh called on the parliaments of the world to choose one language, existing or new, and one script, to be taught in every school beside the mother tongue. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá repeated the principle in almost every list of his Father’s teachings, and these readings collect his statements: language is “the great barrier between nations”; an auxiliary language would remove misunderstanding and save years of study; diversity of native tongues is to remain. A group of readings records his encouragement of Esperanto and his frank judgment that it was not yet adequate and that no single person can make a universal language. Scripture frames the subject with two scenes, Babel and Pentecost, and with Zephaniah’s “pure language.” Zamenhof speaks for himself. The cautions are worth having beside a plan of this size: the Qur’án counts the variety of tongues among God’s signs; Goethe and Wittgenstein value what each language holds; Macaulay and Caliban show what a common language becomes when it is an empire’s; Nehemiah mourns a tongue being lost; and Lincoln’s America is a reminder that people who share a language can still go to war.
questions: “Language is the great barrier between nations.” Describe a misunderstanding you have seen that a shared language would have prevented, and one it would not.
Each person is to learn “his native tongue and the universal auxiliary language.” Why two, and what does the plan protect by keeping the first?

Macaulay dismissed whole literatures in favour of his own language, and Caliban cursed in his master’s. What features of Bahá’u’lláh’s proposal (a choice made by all, an auxiliary role) answer the fear of linguistic empire?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá praised Esperanto and also said that no one person can construct a universal language. What does his handling of it show about supporting an imperfect step toward a principle?
Babel and Pentecost: in one, a single language is taken away; in the other, each hears in his own. Which is nearer to what the readings hope for?
“The universal language will completely wipe away all the differences.” People who share a language still fight. What else do the readings pair with it?

outside.why: Without unity of language the oneness of humanity cannot be organized. The Bible remembers a beginning in which the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
And how it ended: let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.

Diversity of language is called a barrier. The Qur’án counts it among the wonders: of His signs is the difference of your languages and colours. How do the readings keep the sign and remove the barrier?
“If there were a Universal Language, how excellent it would be. We could talk with each other.” The crowd at Pentecost: how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
“Language is the great barrier between nations.” Paul: if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
“The real language is deeper than the outer words.” A psalm on a speech that needs no translation: there is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.

Peoples are “deprived of association, fellowship, and the acquisition of knowledge” by diversity of tongues. Dr Zamenhof, who made Esperanto, in 1887: how different would the case be, had we but two languages to learn.
Zephaniah’s promise: then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve him with one consent.
Each person will learn two languages, “his native tongue” and the universal one. The Persian empire wrote to a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, unto every people after their language.
“We need diversity as well.” The Qur’án: We have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another.

One of the existing languages may be chosen. When an empire chose its own for India, the man who drafted the policy wrote: a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. What in Bahá’u’lláh’s plan guards against a common language becoming this?

A universal language, “so that we will not have to acquire so many languages.” Goethe: a man who has no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own. What might be lost if people stopped learning one another’s tongues?

“The function of language is to convey the thought and purpose of one to another.” Paul: I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.

A universal language will remove misunderstandings. The founders of UNESCO in 1945: ignorance of each other’s ways and lives has been a common cause of that suspicion and mistrust between the peoples of the world through which their differences have all too often broken into war.
“A common bond of mental understanding.” Tagore’s prayer for his country: where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls.

Unity of language is one of the forces that bind peoples. Nehemiah felt the other side of that, when a small people’s tongue was slipping away: their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews’ language. How does an auxiliary language protect mother tongues that a dominant language would swallow?
After Adam the present languages did not yet exist; they arose by separation. Genesis gives the place a name: therefore is the name of it called Babel.
Four hungry travellers quarrel over what to buy, each naming the same fruit in his own language. Hobbes: words are wise men’s counters, they do but reckon by them: but they are the money of fools.
“O members of parliaments throughout the world! Select ye a single language.” Tennyson’s vision of the body that might do it: the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
That “the whole earth … be regarded as one country.” John’s vision: a great multitude, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne.
Victor Hugo to a peace congress in 1849: a day will come when all of you, nations of the Continent, without losing your distinctive qualities, will be blended into a superior unity.
The greatest means of unity is “to understand one another’s writing and speech.” Pentecost again: the multitude were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Two languages now, and in time one. Wittgenstein: the limits of my language mean the limits of my world. If each language is a world, what would humanity keep and lose in coming at last to one?

Some peoples cling to their native tongue alone as their glory. Isaiah records how a foreign tongue sounds to those who fear its speakers: a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.
“The seventh candle is unity of language.” Zechariah pictures the nations seeking one another out: ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations.

“Oneness of language creates oneness of heart.” At Pentecost the order was reversed, and oneness of heart came first: they were all with one accord in one place, and began to speak with other tongues.
Thanks to Dr Zamenhof for an effort toward a language for all. Daniel: all people, nations, and languages should serve him.
A universal language would be “one of the great steps towards universal peace.” Another step, proposed by Woodrow Wilson in 1918: a general association of nations.

Esperanto “is not yet perfected.” Any made or borrowed language meets the difficulty that Ben Sira’s grandson noted when he turned his grandfather’s book into Greek: the same things uttered in Hebrew, and translated into another tongue, have not the same force in them. What must an auxiliary language be able to carry, and what may be left to the mother tongue?

“At present, English and French are more necessary.” Caliban to the master who taught him: you taught me language; and my profit on’t is, I know how to curse. What makes the difference between a language learned as a gift and one learned under a master?
“No one person can construct a Universal Language. It must be made by a Council representing all countries.” Proverbs: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

A unifying language, and attention also to one’s mother tongue. The Qur’án on why revelation itself comes in a people’s own speech: We never sent a messenger save with the language of his folk, that he might make the message clear for them.

“The universal language will completely wipe away all the differences from amongst mankind.” Americans of North and South shared one language and one Bible, and Lincoln said of them: a house divided against itself cannot stand. What else, on the readings’ own account, must accompany a common language?
That “East and West … embrace like two passionate lovers.” Jesus: many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down in the kingdom of heaven.

In a dream he “was speaking in a new language that all of us could understand.” Paul on a communication beneath every language: the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

A country whose inhabitants “are all angels and they speak one universal language.” Paul: though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass. What is the language that the readings finally mean?

shortfall: The 58 readings restate a single principle many times, in lists and brief answers, and the guide is read with 36 outside quotations chosen for the distinct points they make; none was added only to reach the number.

esther-unto-every-people-after-their-lan.text: Then were the king's scribes called at that time in the third month, that is, the month Sivan, on the three and twentieth day thereof; and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded unto the Jews, and to the lieutenants, and the deputies and rulers of the provinces which are from India unto Ethiopia, an hundred twenty and seven provinces, unto every province according to the writing thereof, and unto every people after their language, and to the Jews according to their writing, and according to their language

nehemiah-half-in-the-speech-of-ashdod.text: In those days also saw I Jews that had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab: And their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people

isaiah-people-of-a-deeper-speech.text: Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand
